abstract: Cell populations underpin applications ranging from bioproduction and biotherapeutics to microbiome engineering and biocomputing. However, treating them as bulk quantities rather than as structured systems limits our understanding of population-level stability, productivity, and robustness. Cellular populations self-organize into coexisting subpopulations (SPs) representing phenotypically distinct states that emerge from the interplay of biological noise and selective pressures. We propose that networks of interacting SPs constitute a fundamental organizational layer for engineering stable cell population dynamics. Surveying published single-cell studies across bacterial, yeast, and mammalian systems, we show that populations consistently self-organize into a limited number of SPs. This dimensional reduction can be captured experimentally by clustering single-cell data and gives rise to scaling laws that link population structure to collective performance.
